title: Low Tuck Kwong Perkuat Genggaman, Anak Buah Rela Berkorban
article:
JAKARTA, investor.id – Setelah melepas sebagian besar kepemilikannya ke PT Jhonlin Baratama, konglomerat Low Tuck Kwong kembali memperkuat genggaman di PT Bayan Resources Tbk (BYAN).

Salah satu orang terkaya di Indonesia itu memborong 100.001.000 saham Bayan Resources (BYAN) pada 14 Oktober 2026 di harga Rp 11.200 per saham. Sehingga nilai keseluruhannya Rp 1,12 triliun.

Setelah transaksi tersebut, direktur utama Bayan Resources ini jadi menguasai 3.416.667.832 (10,25%) saham BYAN, dari sebelumnya 3.316.666.832 (9,95%) saham.

“Tujuan transaksi, investasi,” kata Low Tuck Kwong dalam laporannya kepada otoritas bursa.

Di sisi lain, anak buah Low Tuck Kwong, Direktur Bayan Resources Lim Chai Hock menjual 100.001.000 saham BYAN miliknya pada 14 Oktober di harga Rp 11.200. Transaksi penjualan Lim Chai Hock ini selaras dengan transaksi pembelian Low Tuck Kwong.

Setelah transaksi itu, Lim Chai Hock jadi mempunyai 987.149.000 (2,96%) saham Bayan Resources, dari sebelumnya 1.087.150.000 (3,26%) saham.

Low Tuck Kwong mencoba memperkuat kembali genggamannya setelah PT Jhonlin Baratama – perusahaan Haji Isam – masuk menguasai 30,25%.

Dengan kombinasi saham yang juga dimiliki Elaine Low, maka Low Tuck Kwong sekarang memegang 32,3% saham emiten batu bara Bayan Resources.

Sementara itu, Bayan Resources (BYAN) akan menggelar rapat umum pemegang saham luar biasa (RUPSLB) pada 23 November 2026. Yang berhak hadiri dalam RUPSLB itu, pemegang saham yang tercatat namanya dalam daftar pemegang saham BYAN per 29 Oktober 2026 pukul 16.15 WIB.

Pemanggilan RUPSLB dilakukan pada 30 Oktober 2026.

title: Emiten Grup Bakrie Umumkan Entitas Mineral Kritis
article:
JAKARTA, investor.id – Emiten Grup Bakrie, PT VKTR Teknologi Mobilitas Tbk (VKTR) mengumumkan pendirian anak usaha bernama PT Indo Pacific Critical Minerals.

“Perseroan telah mendirikan entitas anak dengan nama PT Indo Pacific Critical Minerals (IPСМ) yang didirikan berdasarkan hukum Republik Indonesia, berkedudukan di Jakarta Selatan,” terang manajemen VKTR dalam keterbukaan informasi dikutip Jumat (16/10/2026).

IPCM, sebut manajemen VKTR, didirikan dengan modal dasar sebesar Rp 1 miliar terbagi atas 10.000 lembar saham dengan nilai nominal Rp 100.000 per lembar saham. Dari modal dasar tersebut, telah ditempatkan dan disetor sebanyak 2.500 lembar saham dengan nilai nominal seluruhnya sebesar Rp 250 juta.

Komposisi kepemilikan saham IPCM terdiri dari VKTR sebanyak 99% saham dan PT Bakrie Metal Industries 1% saham.

Manajemen VKTR menjelaskan, pendirian IPCM merupakan bagian dari strategi perseroan dalam membangun ekosistem kendaraan listrik nasional yang terintegrasi dan berkelanjutan, khususnya melalui penguatan rantai pasok mineral kritis sebagai bahan baku utama baterai kendaraan listrik.

Melalui IPCM, perseroan berupaya mengoptimalkan pemanfaatan sumber daya mineral domestik dan memperkuat rantai pasok strategis Indonesia. Langkah ini diharapkan dapat membuka peluang sinergi di sepanjang rantai nilai industri kendaraan bermotor listrik berbasis baterai (KBLBB), termasuk manufaktur kendaraan komersial listrik, baterai, dan layanan pendukungnya.

“Langkah ini juga mendukung peningkatan kapasitas manufaktur, penguatan TKDN, serta transisi energi Indonesia,” pungkas manajemen VKTR.

title: Laba Darma Henwa (DEWA) Melejit 114,5%
article:
JAKARTA, investor.id – PT Darma Henwa Tbk (DEWA) menyampaikan laporan keuangan perseroan untuk periode yang berakhir pada 30 September 2026.

Dalam 9 bulan tahun ini, emiten terkait pertambangan Grup Bakrie ini mencetak laba bersih yang diatribusikan kepada pemilik entitas induk Rp 513,08 miliar.

Secara tahunan (yoy), angka laba bersih itu melonjak 114,5% dari Rp 239,14 miliar di Januari-September 2025.

Namun, mengacu data pada aplikasi Stockbit Sekuritas, laba Darma Henwa jadi sekitar Rp 159 miliar untuk kuartal III-2026 saja. Ketimbang Rp 262 miliar pada kuartal II-2026.

Kembali ke laporan keuangan yang dirilis DEWA, perseroan membukukan pendapatan Rp 5,1 triliun sepanjang 9 bulan 2026. Meningkat 9,6% dari Rp 4,65 triliun.

Pendapatan dari pihak berelasi PT Kaltim Prima Coal Rp 3,58 triliun dan PT Arutmin Indonesia Rp 1,39 triliun. Pendapatan dari pihak ketiga Rp 119,03 miliar.

Sedangkan, beban pokok pendapatan kenaikannya bisa ditahan hanya 2,2% jadi Rp 4,06 triliun, dari Rp 3,97 triliun.

Alhasil laba bruto Darma Henwa mampu melambung dari Rp 673,15 miliar ke posisi Rp 1,03 triliun.

Per 30 September 2026, total aset DEWA Rp 18,13 triliun dan liabilitas Rp 9,86 triliun.

Untuk kas dan setara kas posisinya menjadi di Rp 744,92 miliar pada 30 September 2026, dibandingkan Rp 1,59 triliun per 31 Desember 2025.

Saham Darma Henwa merosot 7,88% ke Rp 304 pada Kamis (15/10/2026), namun diam-diam investor asing menyerok saham ini dengan net buy Rp 8,65 miliar.

title: Rosatom Signs Deal for 200 MW Floating Nuclear Power Project in Indonesia
article:
Jakarta. North Maluku is poised to become Indonesia’s first province to receive nuclear-generated electricity under a proposed 200-megawatt floating power project involving Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom.

Rosatom has signed an agreement with Indonesian company Pembangkit Listrik Nuklir to supply 200 megawatts of electricity from floating nuclear power units to North Maluku, in a project aimed at expanding power supplies in eastern Indonesia.

The agreement was signed on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week in Moscow on Friday. The two companies plan to deploy two floating nuclear power units to serve northern Halmahera Island.

The project would use Rosatom’s FPU-100 units, each with a generating capacity of 100 MW and equipped with RITM-series marine reactors. Rosatom said the units could begin supplying electricity to Indonesian consumers within five years after the key terms of the power supply contract take effect.

Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev described the agreement as a milestone in energy cooperation between Russia and Indonesia, calling it the world’s first export agreement for electricity supplied by a floating nuclear power unit.

“Cooperation between Rosatom and Indonesia is progressing rapidly. Our recent meeting with President Prabowo Subianto reaffirmed that this world’s largest island nation is consistently pursuing a course toward strengthening energy security and achieving carbon neutrality,” Likhachev said in a statement.

He said Rosatom was ready to offer advanced, proven technologies, adding that the agreement laid the foundation for a long-term partnership.

“I am convinced that this will send a strong signal to the global business community: with systematic government support, the private sector is actively taking the lead in initiating nuclear infrastructure projects capable of transforming the country’s economy,” he added.

Yudi Utomo Imardjoko, director of Pembangkit Listrik Nuklir and an Indonesian nuclear scientist, said the project was intended to support Indonesia’s energy transition and meet growing electricity demand, particularly in eastern regions.

“Leading Indonesia’s energy transition is our foremost objective and responsibility as a national investor. We firmly believe that providing our people with clean, reliable and carbon-free electricity is essential to securing Indonesia’s long-term energy future,” Yudi said.

He said nuclear power could help meet rising electricity demand while supporting economic development, particularly in eastern Indonesia. He added that the project was structured as a business-to-business (B2B) initiative funded by private-sector investment, without relying on the state budget (APBN).

Investor Haji Romo Nitiyudo Wachjo, also known as Haji Robert, welcomed the agreement and thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin, Rosatom and the Russian delegation for their cooperation.

He also expressed appreciation to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin for entrusting him and Yudi with the responsibility of advancing the 200 MW project in North Halmahera, North Maluku.

Wachjo, an Indonesian mining entrepreneur of Javanese-Australian descent, is known as the owner of Indotan Group.

Indonesia has included nuclear power in its national energy planning as part of efforts to strengthen energy security and achieve its target of carbon neutrality by 2060.

Prabowo has discussed cooperation on the peaceful use of nuclear energy with Russian officials, including Putin during a visit to Moscow in July 2024 and Likhachev in May 2026.

The discussions have covered nuclear power development, infrastructure, workforce training and non-energy applications of nuclear technology.

Rosatom has proposed a two-stage approach to developing nuclear power in Indonesia, beginning with small-scale floating nuclear power units before moving to land-based plants equipped with larger reactors.

The proposed North Maluku project would represent a step toward the first stage of that plan. However, the agreement does not establish whether all necessary regulatory approvals, financing arrangements, and implementation requirements have been finalized.

Rosatom says its FPU-100 units are designed to provide continuous electricity to remote coastal communities and industrial facilities. Each unit would use RITM-200M reactors, which the company says are more compact and offer higher power output than earlier marine reactor designs.

Russia has operated the Akademik Lomonosov, the world’s first floating nuclear power plant, in the Arctic region of Chukotka since 2020. The plant uses two KLT-40S reactors and has generated nearly 1.4 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity, according to Rosatom.

The company is also developing floating nuclear units for industrial customers in Russia and building a small-scale nuclear power plant in Uzbekistan using RITM-200N reactors.

Rosatom says it is constructing 27 nuclear power plants in nine countries, making it a major supplier of nuclear technology to overseas markets.

title: Indonesia Says Subsidized Fuel Stocks Cover 16–18 Days
article:
Jakarta. Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia has assured the public that Indonesia’s national fuel supplies remain secure, as reports of shortages emerge in Bali and Manado, North Sulawesi.

Bahlil said stocks of subsidized Pertalite gasoline, which has a research octane number (RON) of 90, were sufficient for 16 to 18 days of consumption. Diesel and gasoline with an RON of 92 or higher had reserves covering 18 to 20 days, he said.

He stressed that Pertalite stocks covering less than 20 days did not necessarily indicate a shortage or a breach of minimum reserve requirements.

“Sixteen to 18 days does not mean we are below the minimum standard. That level is still fine,” he said.

To prevent distribution delays from disrupting regional supplies, Bahlil said he had instructed state-owned energy company Pertamina to increase the number of fuel tankers serving affected areas.

One priority is to accelerate shipments from East Java to Bali and other regions that depend on maritime transport for fuel deliveries.

“I have instructed them to immediately double the number of ships to prevent undesirable situations in the regions and speed up distribution,” Bahlil said.

Pertamina has begun sending additional gasoline supplies to Bali and instructed dozens of gas stations to operate around the clock until distribution returns to normal.

Pertamina Patra Niaga, the company’s fuel distribution subsidiary, previously announced plans to deliver approximately 57.9 million liters of gasoline to Bali between Oct. 14 and 17.

The company has also reinforced distribution operations by deploying additional fuel trucks and drivers, including personnel and vehicles brought in from East Java.

In North Sulawesi, Pertamina Patra Niaga’s Sulawesi regional office attributed long queues at gas stations to delays in the arrival of fuel tankers at local supply terminals. The company expects the situation to ease and gradually return to normal within two to three days.

A fuel tanker carrying 3,000 kiloliters of Pertalite arrived in North Sulawesi on Oct. 13, with an additional 5,000 kiloliters scheduled to arrive on Friday.

The additional shipments and distribution measures are intended to ease local supply pressures and prevent logistical bottlenecks from developing into prolonged shortages.

title: Indonesia Fines DSSA, BREN and CUAN Rp 2.1 Trillion for Market Violations
article:
Jakarta. The Financial Services Authority (OJK) has imposed a combined Rp 2.1 trillion ($117 million) in administrative fines on three listed companies for capital market violations, raising fresh concerns about transparency in Indonesia’s stock market.

The companies are Sinar Mas Group’s Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), which was fined Rp 1.5 trillion; Barito Group’s Barito Renewables Energy (BREN) and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi (CUAN) were fined Rp 500 billion and Rp 100 billion respectively.

All three stocks had previously been included on the regulator’s High Shareholding Concentration (HSC) list, which identifies stocks with highly concentrated ownership.

Hasan Fawzi, OJK’s executive head of capital market, derivatives and carbon exchange supervision, said an investigation found evidence of stock price manipulation involving DSSA, as well as indications of violations in the public offering processes of BREN and CUAN.

“Of the 61 stocks included on the HSC list, 31 have undergone examinations and have shown indications of potential capital market criminal violations,” Hasan told a news conference in Jakarta on Friday.

The findings come amid pressure on Indonesia’s benchmark Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) and scrutiny of the country’s market standards by global index provider MSCI. OJK did not directly link the three companies’ cases to the JCI’s decline.

OJK found evidence of market manipulation involving individual and institutional investors trading DSSA shares through several securities brokerage firms between 2023 and 2026.

The transactions were allegedly carried out in a planned and coordinated manner, resulting in a significant increase in the company’s share price, Hasan said.

To investigate the case, OJK requested data and documents from the securities firms involved and traced the flow of funds among parties connected to the transactions.

The regulator also summoned 12 securities company directors, 15 individuals, and 11 foreign legal entities as part of its investigation.

OJK said it had uncovered evidence of violations by securities company directors and suspended the licenses of those involved.

The investigation concerns alleged breaches of Articles 91 and 92 of Indonesia’s Capital Market Law, as amended by the Financial Sector Development and Strengthening Law, known as the P2SK Law.

In separate examinations of BREN and CUAN’s public offerings, OJK found that shares had allegedly been earmarked from the outset for groups linked to the companies’ controlling shareholders.

The regulator also identified indications of misleading practices in the share allocation process. Several parties linked to the controlling shareholders allegedly received large allocations while concealing their identities.

This resulted in share ownership being concentrated among certain groups, limiting the number of shares available for trading on the open market.

As part of its investigation, OJK requested data and documents from four securities firms that acted as underwriters and three custodian banks.

The regulator also traced fund flows and summoned parties suspected of involvement, including five securities company directors, representatives of three custodian banks, and seven parties linked to the fixed-allocation process.

title: 'MSCI is Not Always Right’: Indonesia Tells Investors to Calm Down
article:
Jakarta. The government seeks to restore calm to the equity market following MSCI’s panic-inducing downgrade plans on Friday, with senior deputy economic minister Dradjad Hari Wibowo reminding investors not to take what the American index provider says at face value.

Indonesian stocks even fell 11.57% after MSCI proposed to slap the low-tier “frontier” market on Jakarta. The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) also saw a temporary trading halt following the sharp sell-off.

Dradjad urged investors to make a comprehensive analysis of the market and gains before rushing into panic mode.

“Yes, MSCI has a high reputation. We indeed have to pay attention to what they say, but they are not always right,” Dradjad told the press, even pulling a printed version of an article uploaded by the Frankfurt-based exchange organization Deutsche Börse.

The 2025 article was titled “Five reasons why the MSCI World is not a perfect investment”, which quoted investor fund analyst Ali Masarwah. The expert pointed out that Germany’s DAX gained 15.5% at a time when the MSCI World Index — which captures large- and mid-cap representatives across developed markets — sank 3.7%.

Dradjad went on to say that this shows that “not everything that MSCI does is beneficial for investors”.

“We will continue to pursue reforms regardless of MSCI’s decision,” Drajad, who had only spent two weeks in the cabinet, said.

“It’s not that we are being stubborn. We will fix what needs to be fixed. We will implement concrete steps. We have been enforcing capital market laws, and we will continue to do so.”

He urged domestic investors to “do the calculations and not easily panic”.

Drajad’s boss Airlangga Hartarto trumpeted Indonesia’s “strong fundamentals” when pressed about the reclassification, saying that the proposed downgrades “had been playing with the market sentiments”.

The sudden announcement has taken the government by surprise, according to Airlangga, saying that MSCI did not mention the reclassification during the recent high-level talks with finance chief Suahasil Nazara in Bangkok.

“We hope investors can tell sentimentals and fundamentals apart. ... Why do other agencies not question [our market]? Why is it always the MSCI that is systematically giving us a deadline?” Airlangga said.

Earlier this year, MSCI threatened to reclassify Indonesia’s status from “emerging” to a “frontier” market.

The current “emerging” status means the equity market has a bigger size and liquidity, with doors wide open to foreign ownership. Markets in the “frontier” group are smaller in the aforementioned criteria. The “standalone” status is worse than the “frontier” label, as it would exclude Indonesian stocks from indices tracked by global funds, hence possibly fueling a multi-billion-dollar capital outflow.

MSCI is set to announce its final decision by the end of June 2027. It is open to changing its mind if Indonesia shows meaningful improvements. The IDX intends to seek further clarification.

Southeast Asia’s biggest economy has spent the year reforming its equity market, among others, by disclosing the names of shareholders with at least 1% ownership after MSCI flagged transparency issues. Jakarta was expecting MSCI to release its review next month.

title: Rupiah Buckles Under MSCI Pressure, Sinks Past Rp 18,000
article:
Jakarta. Rupiah weakened past the Rp 18,000 per US dollar mark on Friday as MSCI’s proposal to downgrade Indonesia’s market status intensified concerns over market governance and trading integrity, adding to pressure from elevated oil prices and a firm US dollar.

Rupiah closed down 89 points, or 0.50%, at Rp 18,027 per dollar on Friday, compared with Rp 17,938 in the previous session.

Traze Andalan Futures director Ibrahim Assuaibi said the currency came under pressure as investors assessed MSCI’s proposal to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to a standalone market. The proposal reflects persistent concerns over market governance and alleged coordinated trading practices, with a final decision scheduled for June 30, 2027.

“Despite various reforms, MSCI has highlighted weak enforcement and market dysfunction,” Ibrahim said in a statement on Friday.

External factors also weighed on the rupiah, even as signs of easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East offered some relief. US President Donald Trump was reportedly considering lifting sanctions on certain vessels in the so-called shadow fleet that transports oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela.

The move is intended to ease global shipping rates, which have reached record highs, a US official said on Wednesday.

However, tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, alongside fresh attacks on vessels in the region, continued to support elevated oil prices and underpin the US dollar.

The rupiah also faced pressure from shifting expectations over US monetary policy. Several Federal Reserve officials have indicated that an interest rate hike in the near term is not considered urgent.

“Investors are now awaiting comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok for clues ahead of the Fed’s meeting later this month,” Ibrahim said.

According to Bloomberg data as of 3:59 p.m. Jakarta time, the Singapore dollar stood at Rp 14,078, while the Japanese yen traded at Rp 114.10. The Australian dollar was at Rp 12,547 and the euro at Rp 20,270.

title: Indonesian Stocks End at 2026 Low After Losing 11.57% on MSCI Warning
article:
Jakarta. Indonesian stocks suffered a massive sell-off on Friday, losing 678 points or 11.57% to close at 5,185, their lowest level this year, after MSCI warned it could reclassify Indonesia from an Emerging Market to a Standalone Market.

Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) traded in negative territory throughout the session, moving between 5,185 and 5,404. The benchmark had started 2026 on a strong footing, hitting a record high of 9,134 on Jan. 20 before entering a prolonged correction.

Trading volume reached 68.57 billion shares, with turnover of Rp 31.95 trillion ($1.77 billion) across more than 2.1 million transactions. Only 10 stocks advanced, while 775 declined and 10 remained unchanged.

Pilarmas Investindo Sekuritas said MSCI's warning had drawn significant attention from market participants because a reclassification could lead to Indonesian stocks being excluded from major MSCI indexes used by global investors as investment benchmarks.

“Investors' concerns mainly relate to ownership transparency, free-float measurement and allegations of coordinated trading practices,” Pilarmas wrote in its research note on Friday.

However, the brokerage said Indonesia's status change was not yet final. MSCI is scheduled to announce the outcome of its evaluation and any reclassification decision by the end of June 2027.

Chief of Economic Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto attributed Friday's market turmoil, including the trading halt and the rupiah's slide to around Rp 18,000 per US dollar, to MSCI's plan to reconsider Indonesia's market classification.

“First, this was certainly triggered by MSCI's announcement, but the announcement came earlier than expected. They had actually promised to make it in November, but it came in October,” Airlangga told reporters at the Coordinating Economic Affairs Ministry on Friday.

Airlangga said MSCI had given Indonesia a window between April and June 2026 to address concerns about its capital market. He stressed that regulatory reforms must be implemented consistently, a process that requires time.

“However, this is a lesson for us going forward: reforms must be implemented, and their progress must be visible, particularly to domestic and foreign investors,” Airlangga said.

“On other technical matters, we will discuss them with the stock exchange and expect concrete measures to be accompanied by a clear timeline,” he added.

Fakhrul Fulvian, chief economist at Trimegah Sekuritas Indonesia, said MSCI's consultation on a potential reclassification raised questions that extended beyond the benchmark's daily performance.

“This is not simply a matter of the JCI falling. When MSCI begins questioning whether Indonesia still deserves to be classified as an Emerging Market, what is being tested is confidence in our market institutions,” Fakhrul said.

He said MSCI's concerns had not emerged suddenly. Since early 2026, MSCI has flagged opacity in share ownership structures, insufficient information to accurately assess free float and concerns about potential coordinated trading behavior that could undermine proper price formation.

“Therefore, in my view, this is no longer just a free-float problem. It has become a problem of trust,” Fakhrul added.

Beyond domestic market concerns, Pilarmas said stronger-than-expected US economic data had increased expectations of further interest-rate hikes. Nevertheless, market participants saw a roughly 72% probability that the Fed would keep rates unchanged at its meeting this month.

The October 2026 edition of the Fed's Beige Book offered a mixed picture of the US economy, reporting moderate growth across most Federal Reserve districts despite persistently high interest rates.

Meanwhile, elevated oil prices added to concerns about inflation and the possibility of tighter monetary policy. Investors were also awaiting China's economic data, including gross domestic product growth figures, scheduled for release next week.

The sharp decline in Indonesian stocks contrasted with gains across most Asian markets, which rebounded after Wall Street ended its previous session higher. Easing selling pressure on technology stocks helped support global sentiment following the previous day's sell-off.

South Korea's benchmark Kospi rose 2.1% to 5,668 after tumbling 7.6% a day earlier as AI-related stocks came under pressure. Japan's Nikkei gained 1.4%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index advanced 0.4%, while the Shanghai Composite edged up 0.2%.

title: MSCI Concerns Put Indonesia’s Market Reforms to the Test
article:
Jakarta. Indonesia’s efforts to improve stock-market transparency face a critical test as global investors question whether regulatory reforms have translated into meaningful improvements in market governance and integrity.

“The announcement of policies and regulatory changes alone is not enough to maintain market confidence,” Nafan Aji Gusta, senior market analyst at Mirae Asset Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe. “Global investors need evidence that ownership structures are becoming more transparent, free float genuinely reflects shares available for trading, and market manipulation is consistently addressed when proven.”

In a Friday review, Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia said market participants continued to question the consistency of Indonesia’s reform progress, citing opaque ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading. According to Kiwoom’s summary of MSCI’s assessment, investors also questioned the lack of meaningful evidence of law enforcement against suspected coordinated trading.

One priority is transparency over ultimate beneficial ownership, which helps identify the parties ultimately controlling shareholdings. Regulators also need to improve free-float disclosures and strengthen oversight of concentrated ownership and suspicious transactions.

These measures are particularly important because reported market capitalization does not necessarily reflect how much stock is genuinely available to investors. Indonesia’s plan to raise the minimum free-float requirement to 15% is intended to improve market investability, but Nafan said announced reforms had yet to demonstrate consistent and significant improvements across the market.

Responsibility rests with the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), the Financial Services Authority (OJK), the Indonesia Central Securities Depository (KSEI) and the government to deliver measurable improvements.

“Regulators need to respond with concrete, measurable steps that international investors can verify,” Nafan said, adding that engagement with MSCI and global investors should be backed by evidence of reform implementation rather than policy commitments alone.

title: Indonesia Surprised by MSCI Downgrade Despite Bangkok Talks
article:
Jakarta. Senior economic minister Airlangga Hartarto admitted Friday that the Indonesian government was taken aback by MSCI’s latest announcement, saying that he found it strange that the index provider did not bring it up during the Bangkok talks.

MSCI announced early in the morning that it was mulling downgrading Indonesia’s status to a “standalone” market. Southeast Asia’s biggest economy had spent the past months convincing MSCI to drop the earlier “frontier” market reclassification by pursuing major market reforms.

“This leaves a big question mark. [MSCI] did not bring up this [issue] when they met [our authorities] in Thailand. And it hasn’t been a week [since their meeting], but then again, let's see. We must not hold negative suspicions,” Airlangga told the press in his office.

Airlangga did not go into detail on the Bangkok meeting, but claimed that Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara and Bank Indonesia Governor Destry Damayanti had met with MSCI high-level officials. They had traveled to the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meeting.

Local news outlet Katadata reported that sovereign fund Danantara held a roundtable with MSCI representatives and Suahasil there. Bank Indonesia deputy governor Thomas Djiwandono was in the room.

MSCI moves have been putting Indonesian equities under stress since earlier this year after the American finance firm weighed a “frontier” status, hence possibly kicking Jakarta out of the “emerging” market group.

Frontier markets have smaller stock markets and lower liquidity, while the “emerging” ones are said to offer greater investment opportunities. The “standalone” status refers to countries that MSCI has to take out of its classifications following serious market accessibility and functioning problems.

At home, Jakarta has been trying to reform its capital market to change MSCI’s mind. This includes disclosing names of shareholders with at least 1% ownership and imposing 15% minimum free float rule.

In a statement responding to the “standalone” threat, financial watchdog OJK chief Friderica Widyasari Dewi said that the domestic capital market would “remain attractive”, citing Indonesia’s “well-maintained economic fundamentals”.

MSCI has now given Indonesia time until the end of June 2027. It has begun accepting feedback from market participants until April.

title: Indonesia Could Join Zimbabwe, Palestine in MSCI Standalone Market Downgrade
article:
Jakarta. Indonesia risks being grouped with Zimbabwe and Palestine under MSCI’s Standalone Market classification, potentially cutting the country off from major emerging-market benchmarks and triggering portfolio adjustments by global funds.

“If Indonesia is downgraded by MSCI to Standalone Market status, it will be removed from the MSCI Emerging Markets and MSCI Frontier Markets indexes and placed in the standalone market category, like Zimbabwe and Palestine,” Nafan Aji Gusta, senior market analyst at Mirae Asset Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe on Friday.

However, the proposed reclassification would not automatically force all foreign investors to sell their Indonesian holdings. Passive exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that track the MSCI Emerging Markets index could be required to sell Indonesian stocks once they are removed from the benchmark, while active funds and investors using different benchmarks would not necessarily face the same obligation, Nafan said.

The potential outflows could nevertheless put pressure on large-cap stocks with significant foreign ownership, including major banks, while reduced liquidity and wider bid-ask spreads could amplify market volatility and weigh on the rupiah.

The proposal reflects concerns over the transparency and integrity of Indonesia’s capital market, with MSCI maintaining its plan unless its consultation process uncovers clear evidence of material improvements in market governance and functioning, according to a Friday review by Kiwoom Sekuritas.

MSCI froze some index changes involving Indonesian stocks in January 2026. During its June 2026 Market Classification Review, investors raised concerns about opaque ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading, Kiwoom said, summarizing MSCI’s findings.

“Authorities have announced reforms. However, market participants consider the progress inconsistent. Suspected coordinated trading continues, and there is no meaningful evidence of law enforcement,” Kiwoom said, referring to information from MSCI.

The concerns also explain why a downgrade to Frontier Market status may not be sufficient to reflect the extent of the problems. Under the proposed Standalone Market classification, Indonesia would leave both the MSCI Emerging Markets and Frontier Markets index families.

“Indonesia’s main problem is not technical access, but market integrity,” Kiwoom said.

Nafan similarly argued that Indonesia’s challenge extends beyond market size or trading depth to whether global investors can trust the market’s ownership disclosures, free-float figures and price-formation mechanisms.

“Announcing policies and changing regulations are not enough to maintain market confidence. Global investors need evidence that ownership structures are becoming more transparent, free float genuinely reflects shares available for trading, and market manipulation is consistently addressed when proven,” he said.

MSCI has raised concerns about concentrated shareholdings, ownership transparency and suspected coordinated trading that could undermine fair price formation, as well as the effectiveness of enforcement. Announced reforms, including plans to increase the minimum free-float requirement to 15%, have yet to demonstrate consistent and meaningful improvements across the market, Nafan said.

The proposed reclassification therefore poses a significant test for the Indonesia Stock Exchange, the Financial Services Authority (OJK), the Indonesia Central Securities Depository (KSEI) and the government. Nafan said regulators needed to improve ultimate beneficial ownership disclosure, strengthen oversight of concentrated holdings and suspicious transactions, and demonstrate consistent law enforcement.

He also called for regulators to present verifiable data on reform implementation when engaging with MSCI and global institutional investors, rather than relying solely on policy announcements.

Indonesia still has time to respond. The consultation deadline is April 30, 2027, with MSCI scheduled to make a final decision by June 30, 2027.

Nafan warned that failure to address the concerns could lead to more persistent foreign capital outflows, higher capital costs and greater difficulty attracting long-term investment.

title: MSCI Warning Raises Existential Questions for Indonesia's Stock Market, Economist Says
article:
Jakarta. MSCI's consideration of downgrading Indonesia from an emerging market to a standalone market represents a fundamental test of the country's credibility in global capital markets, rather than merely a threat to stock prices, a leading economist warned on Friday.

Fakhrul Fulvian, chief economist at Trimegah Sekuritas Indonesia, said such a reclassification could severely diminish the Indonesian stock market's relevance to international investors, potentially excluding it from widely tracked emerging-market investment benchmarks.

"This is not simply about whether stock prices will fall. When MSCI begins questioning whether Indonesia still deserves to be classified as an emerging market, what is really being tested is confidence in our market institutions," Fakhrul said in a statement.

He said MSCI's concerns highlighted weaknesses in ownership transparency, insufficient information to accurately assess publicly tradable shares, and the risk of coordinated trading activity that could distort fair market prices.

Global investors, he argued, need reliable and verifiable information about beneficial ownership, the actual number of shares available for public trading, and the concentration of corporate ownership.

"Global markets cannot rely solely on reported free-float figures. Investors want to know whether those shares are genuinely investable and whether ownership structures are sufficiently transparent," he said.

Free float refers to shares available for public trading, excluding holdings that are restricted or controlled by strategic shareholders.

Governance Under Scrutiny

 Fakhrul said regulatory improvements would achieve little without consistent enforcement, emphasizing that investors must be confident that market rules apply equally to all participants.

"Governance is not about how many regulations exist. It is about investors' confidence that those regulations are actually enforced," he said.

He called for stronger trading surveillance, tougher action against market manipulation, improved corporate disclosures, greater accountability among listed companies, and stronger protection for minority shareholders.

According to Fakhrul, MSCI's review is not an assessment of Indonesia's economic growth prospects but of whether its capital market meets the standards required by global institutional investors.

The country's economic fundamentals may not change overnight, he said, but perceptions of investability can deteriorate rapidly when investors begin questioning market transparency and governance.

The consequences could extend beyond equity valuations.

Fakhrul warned that declining investor confidence could prompt investors to demand higher risk premiums, increasing companies' cost of capital and potentially restricting access to financing.

"Ultimately, institutional quality comes at a price. When trust declines, the cost of capital rises," he said.

Reform, Not Defensiveness

 Fakhrul urged Indonesian authorities to use MSCI's consultation period to implement measurable reforms rather than focus narrowly on preserving the country's emerging-market classification.

His recommendations included more transparent beneficial ownership records, detailed and independently verifiable free-float data, closer monitoring of concentrated shareholdings, stronger enforcement against market manipulation, and improved corporate disclosure requirements.

He also stressed the need to strengthen minority shareholder protections and ensure consistent regulatory oversight.

"What we need now is not cosmetic reform. We need reforms that investors can see and trust," he said.

Fakhrul argued that Indonesia's position as one of Asia's largest economies must be matched by capital market institutions capable of meeting increasingly demanding international standards.

"The market is experiencing an institutional shock. The answer is not panic, but institutional reform," he said.

He concluded that investor confidence was a valuable economic asset that could take years to rebuild once lost.

"MSCI is holding up a mirror to Indonesia's capital market. If we don't like what we see, our job is not to argue with the mirror. Our job is to put things right," Fakhrul said.

title: Indonesian Stocks Crash 10.76% by Midday as MSCI Downgrade Fears Mount
article:
Jakarta. Indonesian stocks plunged 10.76% by midday Friday, extending losses after trading resumed following a temporary halt triggered by a sharp sell-off over MSCI’s proposal to downgrade Indonesia’s market classification from Emerging Market to Standalone Market.

Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) fell 630 points to 5,233 at midday. The benchmark had earlier slumped 650.3 points, or 11.16%, to 5,206 after trading resumed, as investors reacted to concerns over the potential reclassification.

Trading volume reached 38.69 billion shares, with turnover totaling Rp 17.33 trillion ($960.37 million) and transaction frequency exceeding 1.35 million. Only 14 stocks advanced, while 771 declined and three remained unchanged.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) halted trading at 8:58 a.m. Jakarta time after the JCI’s decline reached 8%. Trading resumed at 9:28 a.m., with the exchange maintaining its regular trading schedule.

The sell-off followed MSCI’s announcement that it had launched a consultation on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia from an Emerging Market to a Standalone Market.

MSCI said it would announce its final decision on the proposal no later than the end of June 2027. During the consultation period, the index provider may also issue updates based on feedback from market participants.

Reza Priyambada, an analyst and director at Reliance Sekuritas, said news of the proposed reclassification had triggered a negative reaction in Indonesia’s stock market.

International institutions’ assessments can influence foreign investors’ perceptions of Indonesia’s investment appeal, Reza said, even as the government and market participants maintain that corporate and domestic economic fundamentals remain sound.

“Although the government and market participants consider corporate and domestic economic fundamentals to be sound, negative perceptions from international institutions could still shake investor confidence,” Reza said.

He added that investors could interpret a shift from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status as a downgrade signaling that Indonesia had become less attractive as an investment destination.

Reza said capital market authorities, particularly the IDX and the Financial Services Authority (OJK), should address fundamental issues that have drawn scrutiny from global investors.

“Market reforms should not focus solely on market development and the enforcement of sanctions. Authorities also need to ensure a level playing field in market mechanisms and address other issues that shape international investors’ assessments of the quality of Indonesia’s capital market,” he said.

title: Explainer: What Is MSCI Market Classification and Why Does It Matter for Indonesia?
article:
Jakarta. MSCI groups stock markets into developed, emerging, frontier and standalone categories based on economic development, market size, liquidity and accessibility. The classifications influence how global investors allocate capital and could have significant implications for Indonesia.

Global index provider MSCI plays a major role in how international investors assess and invest in stock markets. Its market classifications help determine which countries are included in its benchmark indexes, which are tracked by investment funds worldwide.

A change in classification can prompt funds to adjust their portfolios, potentially triggering significant buying or selling of stocks.

Indonesia, currently classified as an emerging market, faces the prospect of being downgraded to standalone status after MSCI raised concerns about opaque share ownership, suspected coordinated trading, and persistent market-access problems.

Here is how the classification system works and why it matters.

MSCI conducts an annual review of equity markets worldwide, assessing three main criteria.
• Economic development: MSCI uses this criterion only to determine whether a market qualifies as developed.
• Size and liquidity: The provider assesses whether stocks meet minimum market-capitalization and liquidity requirements for its global standard indexes.
• Market accessibility: MSCI evaluates how easily international investors can buy and sell shares, move capital across borders, and obtain reliable market information.

Accessibility assessments consider factors such as foreign ownership restrictions, capital controls, trading and settlement systems, and transparency.

MSCI also gathers feedback from international investors about their experience operating in each market. Economic growth alone does not guarantee a higher classification if investors face persistent barriers to trading or moving money.

What Are the Four Market Classifications?
• Developed Markets

 These markets generally have advanced economies, deep and liquid stock markets, efficient trading infrastructure, and high accessibility for foreign investors. Developed-market stocks offer investors broad exposure to companies across industries and investment styles, supported by relatively mature market infrastructure. Examples include the United States, Japan, Australia, Singapore, and major Western European markets.
• Emerging Markets

 Emerging markets offer substantial investment opportunities but may have greater regulatory restrictions, operational challenges, or market risks than developed markets. Their investment appeal often comes from economic expansion, industrialization, and growing corporate earnings. However, returns can be particularly sensitive to country-specific factors, including policy changes, currency movements, and foreign investor sentiment. Examples include China, India, Taiwan, Brazil, South Africa, and Indonesia.
• Frontier markets

 Frontier markets generally have smaller stock markets, lower liquidity, and more limited investment opportunities than emerging markets. They can offer exposure to less-developed investment markets, but thin trading volumes and limited accessibility may make it harder for institutional investors to buy or sell large positions without affecting prices. Examples include Vietnam, Morocco, Jordan, and Kenya.
• Standalone Markets

 Standalone markets fall outside MSCI's developed, emerging, and frontier market classifications. The category includes markets that have not been admitted to the main groups and those that have been removed because of significant problems with accessibility or market functioning. A downgrade to standalone status can have greater consequences than a move from emerging to frontier status because a market may lose representation in MSCI's mainstream global equity indexes. Argentina and Pakistan have previously been classified as standalone markets after being removed from the emerging-market category.

MSCI introduced an advanced frontier market subcategory in its 2025 review. It identifies frontier markets with relatively strong accessibility but insufficient market size or liquidity to qualify as emerging markets. The subcategory has specific requirements for accessibility ratings and capital-flow restrictions.

Many investment funds use MSCI indexes as benchmarks or directly track them. A market's classification therefore influences how these funds allocate money across countries.

If a country is removed from an index, funds tracking that benchmark may need to sell affected stocks and redirect capital to eligible markets. The scale of the impact depends on the indexes involved, their implementation schedules and individual fund mandates.

Not all foreign investors follow MSCI indexes, so reclassification does not automatically mean that every investor will sell.

However, anticipated changes can concentrate trading around index-rebalancing dates, increasing trading volumes and potentially affecting share prices and transaction costs.

Classifications also influence portfolio construction. MSCI research covering data through April 2026 found that country-specific factors accounted for 60% to 90% of stock-return dispersion in emerging markets for much of the period studied. In frontier markets, the share was around 85% to 95%.

By comparison, industry and investment-style factors played larger roles in developed markets, where country effects accounted for around 12% to 15% of return dispersion in recent observations.

These differences suggest that political developments, regulatory changes and investor confidence can have a particularly strong influence on emerging and frontier-market stocks.

MSCI has raised concerns about opaque ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading in Indonesia's stock market.

Authorities have responded with reforms, including enhanced disclosure requirements for shareholders with stakes exceeding 1% and a minimum free-float requirement of 15%.

Free float refers to shares available for public trading. A larger free float can improve liquidity and help investors assess the supply of shares available in the market.

However, MSCI has indicated that regulatory changes have not fully addressed market participants' concerns about transparency and trading practices.

In October 2026, MSCI said feedback from investors suggested that downgrading Indonesia to frontier-market status would not adequately reflect the severity of the problems identified. It said it was considering a consultation on standalone status if Jakarta failed to demonstrate meaningful progress by its November review.

title: Bank Indonesia Defends Rupiah as MSCI Review Fuels Selling Pressure
article:
Jakarta. Bank Indonesia has pledged to intensify efforts to stabilize the rupiah after the currency breached Rp 18,000 per US dollar on Friday, as MSCI’s proposed downgrade of Indonesia’s market classification triggered selling pressure on domestic financial assets.

Rupiah opened at Rp 18,038 per dollar, down 100 points or 0.56%, in spot trading on Friday morning, according to Bloomberg data at 9:05 a.m. Jakarta time.

The depreciation followed MSCI’s announcement that it had begun consultations on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to a standalone market, raising concerns over potential foreign investment outflows.

Bank Indonesia’s Head of Monetary and Securities Asset Management Department, Erwin Gunawan Hutapea, said the rupiah’s movements remained broadly in line with regional currencies, with the currency weakening by a limited 0.28% quarter-to-date.

“Foreign exchange reserves also remained adequate at $146.3 billion at the end of September 2026,” Erwin said in an official statement obtained on Friday.

He said the central bank would remain active in the foreign exchange market to maintain the rupiah’s stability in line with economic fundamentals and ensure orderly market mechanisms.

“Interventions continue consistently through offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) transactions, spot and domestic non-deliverable forward (DNDF) transactions in the domestic market, as well as purchases of government bonds in the secondary market,” Erwin said.

Bank Indonesia is also maintaining adequate liquidity, managing interest rate structures in the money market and coordinating closely with corporations, market participants and other relevant parties, he added.

Erwin said rising global risk aversion had strengthened the US dollar and weighed on domestic financial markets, with outflows from domestic portfolio assets expected to continue.

title: OJK Says Indonesian Market Still Attractive After MSCI Threat
article:
Jakarta. The Financial Services Authority (OJK) on Friday tried to cool down market fears after index provider MSCI threatened to further downgrade Indonesia to a “standalone” status.

MSCI had just announced that Indonesia could fall from the “emerging market” group to the “standalone” category, which includes countries with severe market access problems. They are set to make the final decision by the end of June 2027. The announcement quickly caused Indonesian stocks to plunge 8%.

OJK boss Friderica Widyasari Dewi said that the authority “respected” MSCI’s view and independence. The authority will also act on MSCI’s recommendations while striking an optimistic tone.

“We believe the domestic market will remain prospective and attractive,” Friderica said in a statement.

“This is backed by Indonesia’s well-maintained economic fundamentals, an ever-growing investor base, competitive stock valuations, and its issuers overall are still showing positive fundamental performance.”

Indonesian equities had been under pressure since January after MSCI mulled a move to “frontier” status following transparency concerns, hence kicking Jakarta out of the “emerging” group that has more developed and liquid capital markets. Jakarta has been pursuing market reforms to convince MSCI not to forge ahead with the plan. These changes include disclosing names of shareholders with at least 1% ownership and implementing a 15% minimum free float rule.

MSCI wrote that these reforms failed to convince market participants, adding that a frontier market reclassification “would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems”. They will reconsider the move unless there is clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning”.

title: Rupiah Breaks Rp 18,000 as MSCI Review Triggers Market Turmoil
article:
Jakarta. Rupiah weakened past Rp 18,000 per US dollar on Friday as MSCI’s proposal to downgrade Indonesia’s equity market classification to standalone status rattled investor sentiment, adding pressure to an already volatile financial market.

Bloomberg data showed the rupiah opening at Rp 18,038 per dollar in the spot market at 9:05 a.m. Jakarta time, down 100 points, or 0.56%, from Thursday’s close of Rp 17,938 per dollar. The currency had already weakened 35 points, or 0.20%, in the previous session.

The sell-off followed MSCI’s announcement that it had begun consultations on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to a standalone market. The move raised concerns over the country’s standing among global investors and potential implications for foreign investment flows.

The rupiah weakened even as the US dollar retreated from an 18-month high on Thursday. Investors looked past stronger-than-expected US inflation and spending data, shifting their attention to volatility in the shares of artificial intelligence data center companies.

Bank Indonesia (BI) reaffirmed its commitment to stabilizing the rupiah amid global financial market volatility, saying it would maintain a consistent presence in financial markets to ensure orderly trading and keep the currency’s movements aligned with economic fundamentals.

The central bank’s statement came amid concerns over the US inflation data for September 2026, which came in above market expectations and heightened worries that the US Federal Reserve could maintain an aggressive monetary policy stance.

BI’s Monetary and Securities Asset Management Department head Erwin G. Hutapea said the central bank was continuing to optimize its intervention instruments in a measured manner across multiple markets.

“Interventions are being carried out consistently through non-deliverable forward (NDF) transactions in offshore markets, spot and domestic non-deliverable forward (DNDF) transactions in domestic markets, as well as purchases of government bonds in the secondary market,” Erwin said in a statement in Jakarta on Thursday.

Beyond direct intervention in foreign exchange and bond markets, BI is also managing money market interest rates while ensuring adequate banking liquidity. The central bank is stepping up communication with market participants and corporations to curb speculative activity.

title: Indonesian Stocks Plunge 8% as MSCI Weighs Standalone Market Downgrade
article:
Jakarta. Indonesian stocks plunged 8.01% to 5,393 on Friday, shedding 469 points after global index provider MSCI announced a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from an emerging market to a standalone market. Trading was halted for nearly two minutes following the sharp sell-off.

Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) had closed at 5,863 on Thursday, down 1.33%.

The proposed reclassification threatens to trigger foreign capital outflows as Indonesian stocks could be removed from MSCI's emerging market indexes if the change proceeds.

Mirae Asset Sekuritas analyst Wilbert Arifin warned that large-cap stocks and companies with high foreign ownership would be particularly vulnerable. He estimated that the potential outflow of passive foreign funds could reach US$ 3 billion if MSCI implements the reclassification.

MSCI announced the consultation on Oct. 15, New York time, citing concerns over the transparency of share ownership structures and alleged coordinated trading practices that could undermine the investability of Indonesia's stock market.

MSCI has also maintained a freeze on certain changes related to Indonesian stocks in its indexes until further notice while the consultation proceeds, Wilbert wrote in a research note on Friday.

The measures heighten the risk of foreign selling and could add further pressure on the JCI, he said.

“Major banking stocks and companies with high foreign ownership need to be watched closely, as they could be affected if global investors adjust their portfolios in response to a change in classification,” Wilbert added.

However, MSCI has not made a final decision on Indonesia's status. The index provider is accepting feedback from market participants until April 30, 2027, and is scheduled to announce its final decision no later than June 30, 2027.

Amid the uncertainty, Wilbert advised investors to reassess their exposure to large-cap stocks with high foreign ownership. Investors could also consider companies with a larger domestic investor base and relatively lower exposure to index-driven fund outflows.

He stressed that a downgrade was not yet final and that the outcome would depend on tangible improvements in capital market supervision and law enforcement.

Separately, Indonesia's external debt rose to $459.3 billion in August 2026, up 5.6% year-on-year from $454.8 billion in July.

The increase was driven by higher public external debt owed by the government and the central bank, which more than offset a decline in private external debt.

External debt stood at 30.9% of gross domestic product (GDP) in August, with long-term debt accounting for the largest share. While rising debt could increase the government's interest and principal repayment obligations, the dominance of long-term borrowing provides greater repayment flexibility and limits near-term refinancing pressure.

Global sentiment also remained defensive amid growing concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment and whether technology infrastructure companies could generate returns commensurate with their substantial capital spending, Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia said.

On Wall Street, US stocks closed mixed on Thursday. The S&P 500 gained 0.3%, the Nasdaq Composite was relatively flat, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 557 points.

title: PLN Urged to Prevent Blackouts to Protect Investor Confidence
article:
Jakarta. Experts have urged state electricity company PLN's new leadership to improve power reliability, warning that recurring blackouts could deter investment in Indonesia.

PLN appointed Suroso Isnandar to replace Darmawan Prasodjo as president director on Wednesday, following widespread outages in Batam, a major data center and industrial hub. The change comes as sovereign wealth fund Danantara pushes to overhaul PLN's business model and improve efficiency. PLN's Batam subsidiary has also been placed directly under Danantara.

Public policy analyst Trubus Rahardiansah said dependable electricity was essential to Indonesia's target of attracting Rp 2 quadrillion ($111 billion) in investment this year.

"Unstable electricity supply can be a headache for investors," Trubus told the Jakarta Globe, urging Suroso to restore public and international confidence.

The Batam chapter of the Indonesian Economists Association (ISEI) estimated that the outages cost local industry and services Rp 233 billion ($13 million).

Airlangga University economist Rahma Gafmi called for layered backup systems in industrial and export hubs, clear restoration timelines and automatic compensation or billing adjustments for affected customers.

Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR) chief Fabby Tumiwa proposed that PLN concentrate on transmission and distribution while allowing private companies to operate more power plants. He argued that this could ease PLN's financial burden and strengthen service reliability.

PLN remains heavily reliant on government support to keep electricity affordable. In 2025, it recorded Rp 582.68 trillion ($32.4 billion) in revenue and Rp 7.26 trillion in net profit, alongside Rp 87.46 trillion in subsidies and Rp 112.73 trillion in government compensation.

UPN Veteran Jakarta economist Achmad Nur Hidayat said the figures highlighted structural tensions between affordable tariffs and growing investment needs.

"Reducing network investment to improve short-term financial statements may actually increase the risk of future blackouts," he warned.

Danantara Chief Executive Officer Rosan Roeslani said Wednesday that President Prabowo Subianto had instructed the sovereign wealth fund to review PLN's business model and submit recommendations for improving the company's efficiency, productivity and responsiveness.

"The main objective is to accelerate PLN's transformation so that it becomes better, faster and more responsive," Rosan said. "The president also wants to accelerate the development of 100 gigawatts of solar power capacity."

The planned transformation is expected to improve PLN's operational efficiency and productivity while reducing the government's subsidy burden, he added.

Beyond the company's business model, Prabowo also called for a review of PLN's ability to respond to emergencies and unexpected disruptions to electricity supply.

title: Two Years Into Prabowo Presidency, Infrastructure Takes Back Seat
article:
Jakarta. Nearly two years into his presidency, Prabowo Subianto has charted a different development course from predecessor Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, placing costly social programs ahead of the infrastructure expansion that defined the previous decade.

Jokowi pursued ambitious toll-road links from Merak to Banyuwangi and from Lampung to Aceh, as well as Kalimantan’s first toll road. Although the networks remain incomplete, his administration built more than 2,000 kilometers of toll roads, 45 dams and 27 airports.

Under Prabowo, spending has shifted toward free nutritious meals, village cooperatives and schools for disadvantaged children, raising questions about connectivity, logistics costs and growth beyond Java.

The Trans-Sumatra toll road still needs roughly 1,600 kilometers to connect Lampung and Aceh. For 2027, the Public Works Ministry secured Rp 114.59 trillion ($6.4 billion), barely half its Rp 219.81 trillion proposal. Meanwhile, the government allocated Rp 268 trillion to the free meals program in 2026 and earmarked another Rp 240 trillion for 2027.

Bhima Yudhistira, executive director of the Center of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS), said infrastructure’s contribution to jobs and economic activity had weakened as government priorities changed.

“Under Prabowo, the priority has shifted toward social spending,” he said, arguing that infrastructure investment no longer generates the same economic and employment stimulus seen under Jokowi.

The shift is also visible in Nusantara, the planned new capital. Jokowi’s government spent about Rp 75.8 trillion on its development between 2022 and 2024. Prabowo’s administration has committed Rp 48.8 trillion over five years for the next phase, alongside a separate Rp 6 trillion allocation to the Nusantara Capital Authority for 2026.

Bhima questioned progress toward the government’s target of building 3 million homes, citing financially strained state contractors and sluggish mortgage and property lending. “Construction has a significant role in absorbing labor, but that potential has not been fully realized,” he said.

Bernardus Marcello of the Indonesian Economists Alliance (AEI) warned that facilities built for new social programs could divert resources from areas still lacking basic infrastructure.

“These facilities are being developed in areas that are already relatively advanced, while many regions still lack basic infrastructure,” he said.

He pointed to delays on the Trans-Sumatra toll road and slow railway development outside Java. Infrastructure beyond Java, he argued, too often serves mines and resource industries rather than connecting communities to markets and jobs.

Bernardus estimated logistics costs at around 24% of gross domestic product, underscoring the burden on manufacturers and businesses transporting goods across the archipelago.

Danantara Takes Center Stage

 Prabowo has also changed how major projects are financed and managed. Rather than relying primarily on ministry budgets and private participation, his administration has assigned a growing role to sovereign investment agency Danantara, established early in his presidency.

Managing assets valued at roughly $1 trillion, Danantara has been tasked with projects ranging from waste-to-energy plants and a proposed 100-gigawatt solar program to industrial estates, mineral processing, mining, plantations and Jakarta light rail development.

Its investment ambitions also extend overseas, including an Indonesian pilgrimage village in Saudi Arabia and oil-related ventures in Texas.

With hundreds of state-owned enterprises under its umbrella and responsibilities previously held by the State-Owned Enterprises Ministry, Danantara has become central to the government’s development strategy. Its concentration of assets and investment decisions also raises questions about oversight, financial exposure and the balance between commercial returns and public infrastructure needs.

Priorities for the Next Three Years

 Bhima urged the government to focus on projects that directly raise productivity: upgrading industrial estates, supplying renewable power to green industries, developing warehouses for fisheries and plantation processing, and repairing village roads to improve market access.

Bernardus called for stronger public transportation outside Jakarta, irrigation networks, safe drinking water and disaster-prevention infrastructure.

The challenge for the remaining three years of Prabowo’s term, the economists argued, is not simply how much Indonesia spends, but whether investment lowers living costs, creates jobs and connects regions left behind by earlier development.

title: MSCI Mulls Downgrading Indonesia to Standalone Market
article:
Jakarta. Index provider MSCI is mulling downgrading Indonesia to a “standalone” status, which groups countries with severely deteriorated market access.

MSCI had previously threatened to reclassify Indonesia from “emerging market” to a “frontier” one, following concerns over opaque ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading. Indonesian authorities have been pursuing market reforms since then, including enhanced disclosure of shareholders with ownership above 1% and a 15% minimum free float rule.

The reforms, however, failed to convince market participants, according to MSCI, citing market dysfunction and continued coordinated trading. MSCI is now weighing launching a consultation on the standalone market downgrade unless Jakarta shows meaningful progress by the November review.

“Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to ‘frontier markets’ would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems,” an MSCI statement published on Friday reads.

The American finance firm intends to reconsider the plan if the consultation shows “clear evidence of material improvements in market governance and functioning”.

The current freeze on certain index-related changes for Indonesian securities remains in effect until further notice. MSCI will not implement increases to foreign inclusion factors or number of shares.

“MSCI will continue to delete securities identified by the Indonesian authorities under the HSC [high shareholding concentration] framework and to use the 1% shareholder disclosure data to adjust free float estimate.”

Market participants may submit their feedback until April 30, 2027. The final decision is slated to be out by the end of June.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said it would “respect MSCI’s independence in conducting its assessments and classifications based on its methodology”.

“In light of the various advancements and reform measures, the IDX intends to seek further clarification from MSCI regarding the rationale and assessments that underpin the announcement,” the bourse wrote in response to the latest threat.

The Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) has been under downward pressure throughout the year.

Rupiah Ambles Kena Sentimen MSCI, Reformasi Pasar Modal Dinilai Belum Cukup
article:
Reporter:Vatrischa Putri Nur| Editor:Noverius Laoli

KONTAN.CO.ID – JAKARTA. Pengumuman Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) pada Jumat (16/10/2026) menjadi pukulan besar bagi pasar modal Indonesia.

Usulan penurunan status pasar modal Indonesia menjadi sinyal bahwa pembenahan pasar saham domestik belum cukup meyakinkan investor global.

Asal tahu saja, MSCI mengusulkan perubahan klasifikasi pasar saham Indonesia dariemerging marketmenjadistandalone market.

Usulan tersebut berdasarkan hasil penilaian MSCI terhadap transparansi dan tata kelola pasar saham Indonesia, yang belum menunjukkan perbaikan memadai sejak Februari 2026.

Tamparan tersebut tak hanya berdampak pada pasar saham domestik saja. Nyatanya, rupiah pun ambruk cukup signifikan.

Rupiah melemah tajam pada perdagangan Jumat (16/10) menjadi Rp 18.027 per dolar Amerika Serikat (AS), melemah atau 0,50% secara harian. Dalam sepekan, kurs rupiah spot melemah 0,71%.

Ekonom Center of Reform on Economics (CORE), Dipo Satria Ramli, mengatakan sentimen tersebut menjadi tekanan yang cukup berat bagi pasar keuangan domestik.

“Banyak pelaku pasar cukup kaget mengenai isu ini. Banyak yang hanya berekspektasi, ‘Oh, kita dikasihwarningaja,’ dan nggak diancam sampai level ini. Perlu diketahui juga, levelstandaloneini salah satu (klasifikasi) yang paling bawah,” ujar Dipo kepada Kontan, Jumat (16/10/2026).

Memang, banyak investor institusi memiliki mandat investasi yang membatasi penempatan dana hanya pada negara denganstatus emerging market.

Apabila status Indonesia turun menjadi standalonemarket,investor dengan mandat tersebut otomatis harus keluar dari pasar domestik.

“Untuk dampak ke rupiah sendiri, menurut saya ini cukup berat. Karena terutama bagi banyak investor institusi, MSCI ini sebenarnya patokan yang sangat menjadi acuan,” imbuh Dipo.

Tentunya risiko ini yang jadi kekhawatiran, kondisi tersebut membuka potensi arus keluar modal (capital ourflow) cukup besar.

Jika tekanan tersebut berlanjut, rupiah berpotensi kembali tertekan, meskipun besaran pelemahannya masih bergantung pada perkembangan sentimen dan respons pemerintah.

Dipo bilang, persoalan ini tidak bisa diselesaikan hanya dengan mengandalkan intervensi Bank Indonesia (BI).

bank sentral telah menjalankan operasi moneter untuk menjaga stabilitas nilai tukar, langkah tersebut perlu diiringi pembenahan yang mampu memulihkan kepercayaan investor terhadap pasar modal Indonesia.

Untuk diketahui, MSCI sebelumnya menyoroti masalah kelayakan investasi di pasar saham Indonesia dalam evaluasi klasifikasi pasar pada Juni 2026.

Sejumlah persoalan yang disorot mencakup struktur kepemilikan saham yang tidak transparan hingga dugaan praktik perdagangan terkoordinasi.

MSCI mengakui bahwa otoritas pasar modal Indonesia telah mengumumkan sejumlah upaya reformasi. Namun, investor institusi, kata MSCI, menilai penerapannya harus konsisten dan menunjukkan dampak nyata secara berkelanjutan.

Dipo juga sebenarnya mengapresiasi reformasi pasar modal yang dilakukan. Namun menurut dia, pembenahan tersebut belum menjawab seluruh persoalan mendasar yang menjadi perhatian investor.

“Apa yang menjadi isu utama dari pasar itu sendiri adalah masalah likuiditas, harga saham yang bisa digoreng-goreng, dan beberapa hal lain yang masih menjadiconcern.

Jadi, walaupun sekarang sudah transparan dan terbuka, masalah likuiditas dan harga saham yang masih bisa dimanipulasi itu tetap menjadi masalah,” jelas Dipo.

Di tengah ketidakpastian tersebut, Dipo mengatakan arah pergerakan rupiah masih sulit dipastikan karena bergantung pada berbagai faktor, terutama respons pemerintah terhadap ancaman penurunan status pasar Indonesia dan potensi arus keluar modal asing.

Tapi yang jelas, ke depan rupiah dibidiknya masih akan berlanjut menghadapi tantangan dan sulit kembali menguat.

“Pada akhir tahun lalu, rupiah berada di level Rp 16.600 per dolar AS. Saya rasa, untuk kembali ke level per Desember akhir 2025 itu, hingga akhir tahun ini akan sangat-sangat sulit,” pungkas Dipo.

title: Disorot MSCI, Rupiah Terancam ke Rp 18.500 dan Yield SBN Bisa Naik
article:
Reporter:Vatrischa Putri Nur| Editor:Tri Sulistiowati

KONTAN.CO.ID – JAKARTA.Tekanan terhadap rupiah berisiko semakin dalam jika paparan sentimen negatif dari usulan perubahan klasifikasi pasar saham Indonesia olehMorgan Stanley CapitalInternational (MSCI) memicu arus keluar modal asing yang berkelanjutan.

Tak hanya pasar saham dan nilai tukar, tekanan juga perlu diwaspadai merembet ke pasar surat berharga negara (SBN) melalui kenaikan premi risiko Indonesia.

Asal tahu saja, MSCI mengusulkan perubahan klasifikasi pasar saham Indonesia dari Emerging Market menjadi Standalone Market. Usulan tersebut berdasarkan hasil penilaian MSCI terhadap transparansi dan tata kelola pasar saham Indonesia, yang belum menunjukkan perbaikan memadai sejak Februari 2026.

Tamparan tersebut telah berdampak ke rupiah yang ambruk signifikan hari ini. Rupiah melemah tajam pada perdagangan Jumat (16/10) menjadi Rp 18.027 per dolar Amerika Serikat (AS), melemah atau 0,50% secara harian. Dalam sepekan, kurs rupiah spot melemah 0,71%.

Ekonom Universitas Andalas, Syafruddin Karimi, mengatakan tekanan rupiah saat ini lebih serius karena terjadi akibat kombinasi guncangan global dan faktor spesifik domestik.

Reuters mencatat, aksi jual bersih investor asing di pasar saham Indonesia mencapai sekitar US$ 4,7 miliar sepanjang 2026. Di tengah tekanan tersebut, rupiah sempat menyentuh Rp 18.070 per dolar Amerika Serikat (AS), mendekati rekor pelemahan di level Rp 18.190 per dolar AS.

“Meski begitu, pelemahan rupiah belum otomatis berarti krisis eksternal. Level Rp 18.190 menjadi batas psikologis pertama,” jelas Syafruddin kepada Kontan, Jumat (16/10/2026).

Ia memperkirakan bila sentimen MSCI bertahan, indeks dolar AS (DXY) dan imbal hasil obligasi pemerintah AS tetap tinggi, serta arus keluar modal asing berlanjut, rupiah berisiko bergerak ke kisaran Rp 18.200-Rp 18.500 per dolar AS.

Dalam skenario yang lebih buruk, rupiah bahkan berpotensi tertekan hingga kisaran Rp 18.500-Rp 18.800 per dolar AS. Namun, skenario tersebut membutuhkan tekanan tambahan, seperti lonjakan harga minyak, kenaikan imbal hasil global, serta pelebarancredit default swap(CDS) Indonesia.

Syafruddin juga bilang, sentimen MSCI ini secara tak langsung bisa menyasar pasar obligasi negara. Ketika arus keluar asing dari pasar saham meningkatkan permintaan dolar AS, pelemahan rupiah dapat membuat investor obligasi meminta kompensasi lebih tinggi atas risiko nilai tukar. Jika tekanan kurs bertahan, ruang pelonggaran kebijakan moneter Bank Indonesia (BI) juga dapat menyempit.

Imbal hasil atau yield SBN tenor 10 tahun saat ini berada di sekitar 7,17%. Menurut Syafruddin, zona 7,3%-7,5% perlu dipantau sebagai indikasi bahwa tekanan yang bermula dari pasar saham mulai menjalar ke pasar obligasi. Risiko akan semakin besar apabila CDS tenor lima tahun kembali melebar di atas 100 basis poin dan investor asing turut menjual SBN.

Untuk meredam tekanan itu, Syafruddin menyebut respons otoritas perlu dibagi antara upaya stabilisasi pasar dan pemulihan kredibilitas pasar modal. BI perlu menjaga likuiditas valuta asing dan meredam pergerakan rupiah yang berlebihan melalui intervensi di pasar spot, domestic non-deliverable forward(DNDF),offshoreNDF,foreign exchange swap,serta pengelolaan SBN.

Sementara itu, Bursa Efek Indonesia (BEI) dan Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) perlu berfokus pada perbaikan transparansi kepemilikan manfaat ataubeneficial ownership, free floatefektif, kualitas pembentukan harga saham, pengawasan transaksi, serta penegakan aturan terhadap manipulasi pasar.

“Pemerintah juga perlu menjaga konsistensi kebijakan fiskal dan komunikasi agar shock MSCI tidak berkembang menjadi keraguan yang lebih luas terhadappolicy credibility,” tandasnya.

Di tengah volatilitas rupiah, Syafruddin mengingatkan investor untuk lebih berfokus pada manajemen risiko daripada menebak arah pergerakan kurs dalam jangka pendek.

Investor perlu memetakan eksposur dolar AS, termasuk kebutuhan impor, utang valas, pendapatan dalam dolar AS, dan horizon investasi. Perbedaan karakteristik tersebut menentukan kebutuhan lindung nilai atau hedging masing-masing investor.

Sementara itu, investor portofolio perlu mengurangi penggunaan leverage, menjaga kecukupan kas, dan menghindari konsentrasi pada aset yang sensitif terhadap pelemahan rupiah sekaligus kenaikan yield.

Diversifikasi ke aset berpendapatan dolar AS juga dapat membantu mengurangi ketidaksesuaian antara pendapatan dan kewajiban valas. Meski begitu, keputusan investasi tetap perlu mempertimbangkan valuasi dan likuiditas aset.
